cards.front: In what year was the NIA created?
cards.back: 1986, when the National Security Organisation (NSO) was split into the SSS (now DSS), the NIA and the DIA.

cards.front: Which law created the NIA, DSS and DIA?
cards.back: The National Security Agencies Act (Decree No. 19 of 1986).

cards.front: What is the NIA's core responsibility?
cards.back: Maintaining Nigeria's security outside Nigeria on non-military matters: foreign intelligence and counter-intelligence abroad.

cards.front: DSS vs NIA vs DIA: who does what?
cards.back: DSS: domestic security and intelligence. NIA: foreign (external) intelligence. DIA: military intelligence.

cards.front: Who is Director-General of the NIA? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: Ambassador Mohammed Mohammed, appointed 26 August 2024.

cards.front: Who is the National Security Adviser? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, appointed June 2023.

cards.front: Who is Director-General of the DSS? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: Adeola Ajayi, appointed 26 August 2024.

cards.front: Which office coordinates Nigeria's intelligence agencies?
cards.back: The Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA).

cards.front: Who did Mohammed Mohammed replace as NIA DG?
cards.back: Ambassador Ahmed Rufai Abubakar.

cards.front: How many states and LGAs does Nigeria have?
cards.back: 36 states plus the FCT, and 774 local government areas.

cards.front: How many members in the Senate and House of Representatives?
cards.back: Senate: 109. House of Representatives: 360.

cards.front: Name the seven North-west states.
cards.back: Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto, Zamfara.

cards.front: Name the six North-east states.
cards.back: Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Taraba, Yobe.

cards.front: Name the six North-central states.
cards.back: Benue, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Niger, Plateau (plus the FCT).

cards.front: Name the five South-east states.
cards.back: Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, Imo.

cards.front: Name the six South-south states.
cards.back: Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Edo, Rivers.

cards.front: Name the six South-west states.
cards.back: Ekiti, Lagos, Ogun, Ondo, Osun, Oyo.

cards.front: Who is Nigeria's Foreign Minister? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: Ambassador Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, elevated in April 2026 after Yusuf Tuggar stepped down.

cards.front: Who is Minister of Defence? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: General Christopher Musa (rtd), former Chief of Defence Staff.

cards.front: Who is Chief of Defence Staff? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: General Olufemi Oluyede, appointed 24 October 2025.

cards.front: Who are the Senate President and the Speaker? (checked Oct 2026)
cards.back: Senate President Godswill Akpabio; Speaker Tajudeen Abbas.

cards.front: List the stages of the intelligence cycle.
cards.back: Planning and direction, collection, processing, analysis and production, dissemination, then feedback.

cards.front: HUMINT, SIGINT, OSINT: what do they mean?
cards.back: Human intelligence (from people), signals intelligence (from intercepted communications), open-source intelligence (from public information).

cards.front: What is counter-intelligence?
cards.back: Protecting your own secrets, people and systems from foreign spying, recruitment and sabotage.

cards.front: What does “need-to-know” mean?
cards.back: You only get access to classified information that you need for your specific duties, whatever your clearance level.

cards.front: Which Nigerian law protects classified information?
cards.back: The Official Secrets Act (1962).

cards.front: Strategic vs tactical intelligence?
cards.back: Strategic informs long-term policy and planning. Tactical supports a specific, immediate operation.

cards.front: Which zone is the centre of banditry?
cards.back: The North-west, especially Zamfara and Sokoto, plus Katsina, Kebbi and Kaduna.

cards.front: What are the main roots of banditry?
cards.back: Farmer–herder competition, cattle rustling, illegal gold mining, large ungoverned forests and too few police.

cards.front: When were bandit groups declared terrorists?
cards.back: In 2022, by a Federal High Court ruling.

cards.front: What is Lakurawa?
cards.back: An armed group on the Sokoto–Kebbi border with Niger that began as hired protection against bandits, then turned on communities. It mixes crime and jihadist links.

cards.front: North-west banditry in 2025: how many incidents and casualties?
cards.back: 599 incidents and 2,742 casualties, nearly double 2024.

cards.front: What happened in Sokoto on 25 December 2025?
cards.back: US forces struck Islamic State targets, with Nigerian cooperation according to US officials.

cards.front: What did the US designate Nigeria in October 2025?
cards.back: A “Country of Particular Concern” over religious freedom.

cards.front: What happened on the Abuja–Kaduna train in March 2022?
cards.back: Gunmen bombed and attacked the train, killing passengers and kidnapping dozens.

cards.front: Which school was attacked in Niger State in November 2025?
cards.back: St Mary's Catholic School, Papiri: more than 300 pupils and staff were abducted.

cards.front: Which state passed an anti-open-grazing law in 2017?
cards.back: Benue State.

cards.front: Who founded Boko Haram, where and when?
cards.back: Mohammed Yusuf, in Maiduguri, Borno State, around 2002.

cards.front: When were the Chibok girls kidnapped and how many?
cards.back: April 2014: 276 schoolgirls.

cards.front: When did Boko Haram split into JAS and ISWAP?
cards.back: 2016, after the group's 2015 pledge to the Islamic State.

cards.front: How and when did Abubakar Shekau die?
cards.back: May 2021, during a clash with ISWAP fighters.

cards.front: What is the MNJTF and which members remain?
cards.back: The Multinational Joint Task Force against Boko Haram and ISWAP, based in N'Djamena: Nigeria, Chad, Cameroon and Benin. Niger left in March 2025.

cards.front: What is Operation Safe Corridor?
cards.back: Nigeria's de-radicalisation and reintegration programme for ex-fighters, started in 2016 in Gombe.

cards.front: What is the military's North-east operation called?
cards.back: Operation Hadin Kai.

cards.front: When was IPOB founded and by whom?
cards.back: 2012, by Nnamdi Kanu.

cards.front: What sentence did Nnamdi Kanu receive and when?
cards.back: Life imprisonment on terrorism charges, 20 November 2025.

cards.front: What is the ESN?
cards.back: The Eastern Security Network, IPOB's armed wing, formed in December 2020.

cards.front: What is Amotekun?
cards.back: The Western Nigeria Security Network, launched by the six South-west states in January 2020.

cards.front: What was the 2009 Presidential Amnesty Programme?
cards.back: A programme that paid, disarmed and retrained Niger Delta militants.

cards.front: What is the Deep Blue Project?
cards.back: Nigeria's maritime security programme, launched 2021, with ships, aircraft and a command centre to fight piracy in the Gulf of Guinea.

cards.front: What happened in Owo, Ondo State, on 5 June 2022?
cards.back: Gunmen attacked St Francis Catholic Church during Mass; the government blamed ISWAP.

cards.front: When was Niger's coup and who took power?
cards.back: 26 July 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani overthrew President Mohamed Bazoum.

cards.front: Who leads Burkina Faso?
cards.back: Captain Ibrahim Traoré, since the September 2022 coup.

cards.front: Who leads Mali?
cards.back: Assimi Goïta, after coups in August 2020 and May 2021.

cards.front: What founded the Alliance of Sahel States and when?
cards.back: The Liptako-Gourma Charter, signed 16 September 2023.

cards.front: When did the AES exit from ECOWAS take effect?
cards.back: 29 January 2025.

cards.front: Who chaired ECOWAS during the Niger coup?
cards.back: President Bola Tinubu of Nigeria.

cards.front: How did Nigeria pressure Niger after the coup?
cards.back: Border closure, ECOWAS sanctions, cutting electricity supply, and the threat of military intervention. Sanctions were lifted in February 2024.

cards.front: Roughly how long is the Nigeria–Niger border?
cards.back: About 1,600 km, touching Sokoto, Kebbi, Katsina, Jigawa, Yobe and Borno.

cards.front: Which foreign force now backs Mali's junta?
cards.back: Russia's Africa Corps, which replaced the Wagner group in 2025.

cards.front: What happened to 11 Nigerian Air Force personnel in December 2025?
cards.back: Burkina Faso detained them over an unauthorised airspace entry.

cards.front: What is JNIM?
cards.back: Al-Qaeda's Sahel affiliate, formed 2017, active in Mali and Burkina Faso and spreading toward coastal states and Nigeria.

cards.front: Which gas pipeline would link Nigeria, Niger and Algeria?
cards.back: The Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline.

cards.front: When did Russia launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine?
cards.back: 24 February 2022.

cards.front: When did Russia annex Crimea?
Which four Ukrainian regions did Russia claim to annex in 2022?
cards.back: Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

cards.front: What are Russia's main peace demands (2026)?
cards.back: No NATO for Ukraine, Russian control of all of Donbas and parts of Zaporizhzhia, limits on Ukraine's army.

cards.front: Which US envoys carried the September 2026 peace proposal?
cards.back: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Zelenskyy rejected its territorial concessions.

cards.front: What was the Black Sea Grain Initiative?
cards.back: A Türkiye- and UN-brokered deal (July 2022 to July 2023) that let Ukraine export grain by sea.

cards.front: How did Nigeria vote on the March 2022 UN resolution on Ukraine?
cards.back: In favour of the resolution demanding Russia withdraw.

cards.front: Why did the ICC issue an arrest warrant for Putin?
cards.back: Over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children (March 2023).

cards.front: When did the 2026 Iran war begin and how?
cards.back: 28 February 2026, with US and Israeli strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

cards.front: Why does the Strait of Hormuz matter?
cards.back: About a fifth of the world's oil passes through it. Iran closed it in late March 2026.

cards.front: Which country hosted the April 2026 US–Iran talks?
cards.back: Pakistan: the Islamabad Talks, 12–13 April. They failed and the US imposed a naval blockade.

cards.front: What was the Islamabad Memorandum?
cards.back: A 17 June 2026 deal, brokered by Pakistan, that lifted the US and Iranian blockades.

cards.front: When was the US–Iran ceasefire, and when did it collapse?
cards.back: Announced 28 June 2026; collapsed 8 July when Iran attacked commercial ships.

cards.front: Who mediates US–Iran talks now (Sept 2026)?
cards.back: Qatar, with indirect talks in New York during the UN General Assembly.

cards.front: What is the main sticking point in US–Iran talks?
cards.back: Sequencing: Iran wants Hormuz, sanctions and a ceasefire settled first and nuclear talks later; the US wants everything together.

cards.front: Which Iranian allies joined the 2026 war?
cards.back: Hezbollah, Iraqi militias and the Houthis (from 28 March).

cards.front: What was the JCPOA?
cards.back: The 2015 Iran nuclear deal. The US withdrew in 2018.

cards.front: What happened in June 2025 between Israel and Iran?
cards.back: A 12-day war; the US bombed nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan.

cards.front: What happened on 7 October 2023?
cards.back: Hamas attacked southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking about 250 hostages.

cards.front: When did the Gaza ceasefire take effect?
cards.back: 10 October 2025, under President Trump's 20-point plan.

cards.front: What is UN Security Council Resolution 2803?
cards.back: The November 2025 resolution endorsing the Board of Peace and an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.

cards.front: Who chairs the Board of Peace?
cards.back: US President Donald Trump.

cards.front: Which country took Israel to the ICJ for genocide?
cards.back: South Africa, in December 2023.

cards.front: What did the 1993 Oslo Accords create?
cards.back: The Palestinian Authority and a framework toward a two-state solution.

cards.front: Which Western countries recognised Palestine in September 2025?
cards.back: The UK, France, Canada and Australia.

cards.front: What is Nigeria's position on Israel–Palestine?
cards.back: Support for a two-state solution; relations with Israel and recognition of Palestine.

cards.front: How much is the Board of Peace's Gaza reconstruction plan (Sept 2026)?
cards.back: $2.4 billion.

cards.front: Who is fighting in Sudan's war, and since when?
cards.back: Since 15 April 2023: the Sudanese Armed Forces (Burhan) against the Rapid Support Forces (Hemedti).

cards.front: Which Darfur city did the RSF capture in October 2025?
cards.back: El Fasher.

cards.front: Which rebel group took Goma in January 2025?
cards.back: M23, which UN experts say is backed by Rwanda.

cards.front: Define a recession.
cards.back: Two consecutive quarters of falling GDP.

cards.front: Define stagflation.
cards.back: Slow or no economic growth combined with high inflation.

cards.front: What is a tariff?
cards.back: A tax on imported goods.

cards.front: When did Nigeria remove the petrol subsidy?
cards.back: May 2023, at the start of the Tinubu administration.

cards.front: What is the Dangote refinery's capacity?
cards.back: 650,000 barrels per day, near Lagos.

cards.front: When did Nigeria leave the FATF grey list?
cards.back: October 2025.

cards.front: What is Nigeria's status in BRICS?
cards.back: Partner country since January 2025.

cards.front: What is AfCFTA and when did trading start?
cards.back: The African Continental Free Trade Area; trading began 1 January 2021.

cards.front: Since when has Nigeria been in OPEC?
What was AGOA and what happened to it?
cards.back: A US law giving many African exports duty-free access. It lapsed in September 2025.

cards.front: What is Nigeria's main anti-terrorism law?
cards.back: The Terrorism (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022.

cards.front: What does the National Counter Terrorism Centre do and where is it?
cards.back: It coordinates counter-terrorism; it sits in the Office of the National Security Adviser.

cards.front: Which agency tracks terrorist financing in Nigeria?
cards.back: The Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).

cards.front: Which region does the Global Terrorism Index call the epicentre of terrorism?
cards.back: The Sahel, with over half of global terrorism deaths.

cards.front: Name four common drivers of radicalisation.
cards.back: Poverty and unemployment, poor governance, grievances against security forces, lack of education, plus online propaganda.

cards.front: What is Ansaru?
cards.back: A Nigerian jihadist group aligned with al-Qaeda, which split from Boko Haram.

cards.front: When did Nigeria adopt its plan for preventing violent extremism?
cards.back: 2017: the Policy Framework and National Action Plan for Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism.

cards.front: When was NAPTIP created?
What is Nigeria's current anti-trafficking law?
cards.back: The Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act 2015.

cards.front: What is the Palermo Protocol?
cards.back: The UN protocol (2000) to prevent, suppress and punish trafficking in persons.

cards.front: What did the Oba of Benin do in March 2018?
cards.back: He revoked the juju oaths traffickers used to control victims.

cards.front: What is the main trafficking route to Europe?
cards.back: Southern Nigeria → Niger (Agadez) → across the Sahara to Libya → the Mediterranean.

cards.front: Which agency fights drug trafficking?
cards.back: The NDLEA, created in 1989.

cards.front: Which ECOWAS treaty controls small arms?
cards.back: The ECOWAS Convention on Small Arms and Light Weapons (2006).

cards.front: Which law covers cybercrime in Nigeria?
cards.back: The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015, amended in 2024.

cards.front: What are the 4 Ds of Nigeria's foreign policy?
cards.back: Democracy, Development, Demography, Diaspora.

cards.front: Who introduced the 4-D doctrine?
cards.back: Yusuf Tuggar, as Foreign Minister, in 2023.

cards.front: What does “Demography” mean in the 4-D doctrine?
cards.back: Treating Nigeria's large, young population as an asset to be educated, skilled and employed.

cards.front: What does “Diaspora” mean in the 4-D doctrine?
cards.back: Engaging Nigerians abroad for investment, skills and remittances (around $20 billion a year).

cards.front: What is the “concentric circles” doctrine?
cards.back: A 1980s approach ranking Nigeria's interests from its immediate neighbours outward to West Africa, Africa and the world.

cards.front: When and where was ECOWAS founded?
cards.back: 28 May 1975, by the Treaty of Lagos. Its headquarters is in Abuja.

cards.front: When did Nigeria join the UN?
cards.back: 7 October 1960.

cards.front: What was ECOMOG?
cards.back: The ECOWAS peacekeeping force, led by Nigeria, in Liberia and Sierra Leone in the 1990s.

cards.front: What is NiDCOM?
cards.back: The Nigerians in Diaspora Commission, created in 2017.

cards.front: What is the Technical Aid Corps?
cards.back: A scheme (since 1987) sending Nigerian professionals to work in other developing countries.

cards.front: You walk into the interview room. What do you do?
cards.back: Greet the panel and stay standing until you are invited to sit.

cards.front: You don't know the answer to a question. What do you do?
cards.back: Answer anyway: say what you do know, reason out loud, and be honest about uncertainty. Never stay silent.

cards.front: What goes in your self-appraisal?
cards.back: Name, LGA and state of origin, date of birth, schools and qualifications, achievements or awards, work experience.

cards.front: A simple structure for any answer?
cards.back: Point, reason, example, conclusion.

cards.front: A relative asks about your work at the Agency. What do you say?
cards.back: Nothing about the work itself. Discretion is part of the job.

cards.front: Name five qualities intelligence work needs.
cards.back: Discretion, loyalty, integrity, analytical thinking, resilience (also curiosity and languages).

cards.front: When were the Northern and Southern Protectorates amalgamated, and by whom?
cards.back: 1 January 1914, by Lord Frederick Lugard.

cards.front: Who suggested the name “Nigeria”?
cards.back: Flora Shaw (later Lady Lugard), in 1897.

cards.front: Who is called the father of Nigerian nationalism?
cards.back: Herbert Macaulay, who founded the NNDP in 1923.

cards.front: Which colonial constitution made Nigeria a federation?
cards.back: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954.

cards.front: Who was Nigeria's first Prime Minister?
cards.back: Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa (1960–1966).

cards.front: When did Nigeria become a republic, and who was President?
cards.back: 1 October 1963; Nnamdi Azikiwe (ceremonial President).

cards.front: When was Nigeria's first military coup?
cards.back: 15 January 1966.

cards.front: When did the civil war start and end?
cards.back: 6 July 1967 to 15 January 1970.

cards.front: Which head of state was assassinated on 13 February 1976?
cards.back: General Murtala Mohammed.

cards.front: Who was President of the Second Republic?
cards.back: Shehu Shagari, from 1 October 1979 until the coup of 31 December 1983.

cards.front: What happened on 12 June 1993?
cards.back: A presidential election, believed won by M.K.O. Abiola, which Babangida's government annulled. 12 June is now Democracy Day.

cards.front: When did the Fourth Republic begin?
cards.back: 29 May 1999, with President Olusegun Obasanjo.

cards.front: When did Abuja become the capital?
cards.back: 12 December 1991, replacing Lagos.

cards.front: Which Nigerian president died in office?
cards.back: Umaru Musa Yar'Adua, in May 2010. (Abacha also died in office as military head of state in 1998.)

cards.front: Who led the Interim National Government in 1993?
cards.back: Ernest Shonekan.

cards.front: What does Section 14(2)(b) of the Constitution say?
cards.back: The security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government.

cards.front: Which chapter of the Constitution contains fundamental rights?
cards.back: Chapter IV.

cards.front: What is the federal character principle?
cards.back: Appointments and institutions should reflect Nigeria's diversity (Section 14(3)).

cards.front: What is the minimum age to run for President?
cards.back: 35, since the Not Too Young To Run Act (2018).

cards.front: Where do the Niger and Benue rivers meet?
cards.back: Lokoja, Kogi State.

cards.front: What is Nigeria's highest point?
cards.back: Chappal Waddi (about 2,419 m), Taraba State.

cards.front: Where and when was oil first found in commercial quantities?
cards.back: Oloibiri, in present-day Bayelsa State, in 1956.

cards.front: Who designed the Nigerian flag?
cards.back: Michael Taiwo Akinkunmi.

cards.front: What is Nigeria's national motto?
cards.back: Unity and Faith, Peace and Progress.

cards.front: What does the white Y on the coat of arms represent?
cards.back: The Niger and Benue rivers.

cards.front: What is the national anthem since May 2024?
cards.back: “Nigeria, We Hail Thee”, the original 1960 anthem. “Arise, O Compatriots” is now the national song.

cards.front: When was the naira introduced?
cards.back: 1 January 1973, replacing the Nigerian pound.

cards.front: Which four countries border Nigeria?
cards.back: Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon.

cards.front: What happened to the Bakassi Peninsula?
cards.back: It was handed to Cameroon after a 2002 ICJ ruling; handover completed in August 2008.

cards.front: Who was the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
cards.back: Wole Soyinka, in 1986.

cards.front: How many states did Nigeria have in 1967, 1976, 1991 and 1996?
